U.S House passes federal ratepayer protection bill

Following a trend of states, including Oklahoma, that have enacted laws to mitigate the impact of data centers on local utility rates, Congress is moving toward passage of federal legislation.

Alex Cameron
September 16, 2026 09:30 PM
6 min read
1 of 3
2 of 3
3 of 3
WASHINGTON, D.C. -
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:09
Instaread

With near-unanimous support, the U.S. House of Representatives Wednesday night passed the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340), legislation that comes in response to nationwide concerns over the proliferation of data centers and their impact on utility rates. The bipartisan bill was introduced by Representatives Gabe Evans (R-CO) and Kathy Castor (D-FL) and is designed to shield American households and small businesses from rising utility costs driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and the massive data centers needed to support AI.

Lawmakers from both parties pushed for the legislation due to several growing concerns:

  • Preventing “Cost Shifting” to Consumers: Building new data centers requires massive upgrades to electrical grids, including new power plants, transmission lines, and distribution networks. Without legislative safeguards, the billions of dollars required for these upgrades might be passed down to ordinary utility customers, spiking monthly electricity bills for working families, farmers, and seniors.
  • Balancing Innovation with Affordability: Members of Congress recognize that large-scale infrastructure is critical for the U.S. to maintain global leadership in AI technology and compete with nations like China. However, they argue that private tech giants—rather than the American public—should absorb the financial burdens of this growth.
  • Enforcing Corporate Accountability: Major technology companies previously signed voluntary pledges to cover their energy costs. Following the lead of states like Oklahoma, members of Congress decided a federal standard was necessary to give these commitments teeth and protect communities from future liability if a tech company downscales or backs out of an area.

What the Act Would Do

The Ratepayer Protection Act, if signed into law, would amend the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (PURPA) to establish a new federal standard for “large-load customers"—defined specifically as nonresidential facilities (like data centers) that have a peak electricity demand of 100 megawatts (MW) or more at a single site.

  • Mandatory Consideration: State Public Utility Commissions (PUCs) would have one year to commence consideration of the new standard, and two years to make a decision on adoption.

  • New Standard for “large-load customers":

    (A) RECOVERY OF FULL, INCREMENTAL COST OF UPGRADES.—A rate charged, or entered into, by an electric utility for providing electric service to a large-load customer shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer, including in the event of such large-load customer terminating a contract or other agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy, or otherwise ceasing the purchase of electric energy from the electric utility.

    (B) FINANCIAL ASSURANCES AND CONTRIBUTIONS.—Before making any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade that is necessary to serve the load of a large-load customer, an electric utility shall require the large-load customer provide to the electric utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of such upgrade.

    In interviews with Griffin Media Washington Bureau Chief Alex Cameron, Rep. Josh Brecheen (R-OK2) and Senator James Lankford spoke about the legislation:

BRECHEEN: “At the end of the day, what Oklahoma state statute did is going to be the most paramount, because when you compare what the federal legislation will do, it—what the state of Oklahoma rightly did, I believe, was they looked at 75 megawatts. This [federal bill] is at 100MW or comparable. I still have some concerns about what ‘comparable’ means, but the federal legislation is going to say to the states, we want you to look at this 100 megawatt or greater, and then take a position on a large-load tariff to protect your customers from a rate increase. It is right that anybody, as a citizen, should not have to have socialism passed upon them where they have to carry the burden of an activity that others would enjoy the benefit from. In my town halls. I would ask people, hold up your cell phones, and I wanted people to understand that if you are using an app, if you are using cloud, 100% of that activity is going through a data center...the question, Alex, for Congress is — and this is something that I think anybody who is an originalist wants to know — when it comes to commerce among the states, the enumerated powers granted to Congress, among the states, among foreign nations and among the tribes, the authority to get involved. The father of our Constitution, James Madison, made it very plain, as he’s the guy who kept the notes on the Constitutional Convention, that when it came among the states, the federal government was to never be involved to the same level as they could regulate commerce on foreign nations. His exact wording is... ‘regarding commerce among the states, the authority of Congress is to be a negative and a preventative to stop injustice among the states.’ From the context of our Founding Fathers, they wanted free market principles to work. And so ultimately, what this measure will do—it’s going to make sure that state A, who does not make a decision, that they’re not impacting customers in state B as a recipient. Where this gets very difficult, it’s the transmission lines that are connecting all of these states that then the federal government makes an allocation of fault for who’s pulling on most of these data centers at this point, in terms of a large load. That’s why transmission lines are coming online, even accompanied by more data centers. And so FERC is making a decision to pass on those costs up to the state. If they can’t cooperatively agree upon what percentage it is that they have responsibility for. And so, in original intent, as my team and I’ve been scrubbing this, I believe that the federal government, in a very narrow what I believe would be in line with the original intent, the federal government has a role to make sure states—citizenry in one state are not subsidizing activity in another state. That would be unjust.

LANKFORD: “With the data center issue, the first priority is that it actually helps communities, not hurts communities; that should be the baseline for every single community that’s looking at it, a data center. There are some communities that want them; they want the taxes, they want the revenue, they want the jobs coming in — that’s great. A local community should be able to make that decision; they should also be able to get answers out of the questions. But the last thing it should do is to be able to come in and hurt local communities, either with they can’t have water for their agriculture, or their power rates go up for local electricity, which nobody wants. No one wants to see that, nor should see that.

LANKFORD: “On a national level, we don’t wanna have a national zoning requirement, but we do need to make sure, ‘Hey, we’re protecting the rights of consumers and locations...If we’re going to have increased uses of our phone, basically, we’re going to have data centers that are out there because that’s going to go hand-in-hand with the system, but we can’t have it in a situation where it hurts communities and not helps communities.”
